passage: Okay, don't laugh, but there's a boy in the next section who looks at me like I'm made of glass. I'm Gopika. His name is Arnab. He waits by the gate each morning and copies down whatever I say in the canteen queue, and last week he slipped a card into my bag that said I was the most perfect person he knew. Part of me went pink and pleased. Another part felt hot and cornered, like I had to be perfect now. I didn't want to laugh at him or boast to my friends about it. So I found him near the water cooler and said, "Thanks, that was kind. But I'm just a person who forgot her tiffin yesterday. And please don't wait at the gate every day, it makes me nervous." He blushed hard, but he nodded.

qa.q: Where does Arnab wait for Gopika each morning?
qa.a: He waits by the gate.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Gopika have about the card?
qa.a: Flattered and uneasy. Part of her went pink and pleased, and another part felt hot and cornered, as if she had to be perfect now.

qa.q: What did Gopika do that was wise?
qa.a: She thanked Arnab kindly, told him she was just a person, and clearly asked him not to wait at the gate every day.

qa.q: How might Arnab have felt when Gopika spoke to him at the water cooler?
qa.a: Embarrassed, since he blushed hard, but he nodded, so he may have understood. Being seen as a person and not an idol can sting a little before it helps.

grounding: Gopika is flattered and uneasy about a boy who idolises her and kindly tells him she is just a person and sets a boundary.

passage: The school trip bus crawled through monsoon traffic, and the seating chart put Jahnavi right beside Rafiq. Three days ago she had told him how she felt, and he had said, gently, that he didn't feel the same. Her cheeks burned every time the bus jerked and their elbows touched. The windows were fogged, the driver's radio crackled, and there was nowhere to go. She wanted to say something clever, to ask "are you sure?" one more time. Instead she pulled out her earphones, said, "Want one side?" and handed him the other bud. Neither spoke. At the rest stop she sat with Aditi on a wet bench and let herself cry a little into the chai steam. "It hurts," she said. "But I'm glad I said it."

qa.q: What did the seating chart do on the school trip bus?
qa.a: It put Jahnavi right beside Rafiq.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel on the bus, and why did she hold back?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and hurt, her cheeks burning, and though she wanted to ask "are you sure?" again, she knew pressing him would not change his answer, so she shared her earphones instead.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi handle the sting in a healthy way?
qa.a: She accepted his no without pressing, cried a little with her friend Aditi, and said she was glad she had spoken.

qa.q: How might Rafiq have seen the bus ride?
qa.a: Probably awkward too. He may have felt relieved that Jahnavi did not press him, and grateful for the shared earphone.

grounding: Jahnavi was turned down by her crush, feels the sting on a crowded bus, and accepts it without pressing and grieves with a friend.

passage: At the tuition verandah in Bhuj town, Rehana found a folded note tucked in her copy. It was from Zainab, in careful round letters: she liked Rehana as more than a friend. Rehana read it twice, her stomach knotting, and she thought about how easy it would be to smile, say nothing and enjoy being liked. But that wouldn't be fair. After class she asked Zainab to walk with her to the corner shop. "Thank you for telling me. It took courage," she said. "I care about you as my friend. But I don't feel the same way, and I don't want you hoping." Zainab swallowed and nodded. Rehana didn't tell anyone else, and the next day she sat beside her at tuition as usual.

qa.q: Where did Rehana find Zainab's note?
qa.a: She found it folded and tucked into her copy at the tuition verandah.

qa.q: What did Rehana think about before answering the note?
qa.a: She thought how easy it would be to smile, say nothing and enjoy being liked, but felt that wouldn't be fair to Zainab.

qa.q: What made Rehana's answer a kind and clear one?
qa.a: She thanked Zainab for her courage, said plainly she did not feel the same way, and kept it private, so there were no mixed signals and Zainab kept her dignity.

qa.q: How might Zainab have felt when she nodded?
qa.a: Hurt, since she swallowed before nodding, but also perhaps respected, because Rehana was honest and sat beside her the next day. 🤍

grounding: Rehana does not return a classmate's feelings and gives a kind, clear no, keeping her dignity and not leading her on.

passage: Every morning at the bus stop in Buenos Aires, Layla's tongue turned to cardboard when Diego walked up. Her brain ran the film in advance: she says something odd, he raises an eyebrow, the whole bus laughs. So she stared at her phone and said nothing. On Thursday her friend Sofia muttered, "Just ask him about the maths quiz. People talk about the quiz." Layla's palms were damp, but when Diego stopped next to her she blurted, "Did you finish question six?" Her voice cracked on six. Diego laughed, not unkindly. "No, I gave up. Did you?" They spent the ride complaining about question six. She got off at her stop still red in the face, but she noticed she was smiling, and nobody on the bus had cared at all.

qa.q: Where did Layla see Diego every morning?
qa.a: She saw him at the bus stop in Buenos Aires.

qa.q: Why did Layla stare at her phone instead of speaking?
qa.a: She was afraid of embarrassing herself. Her mind ran the film in advance of saying something odd and the whole bus laughing.

qa.q: What small step helped Layla break the silence?
qa.a: She began with ordinary talk by asking about question six of the maths quiz, as her friend Sofia suggested, and accepted that her voice cracking was okay.

qa.q: How might Diego have seen her question?
qa.a: Probably as a friendly, normal thing to say. He laughed but not unkindly, and he joined in complaining about the question. 😊

grounding: Layla freezes near her crush and imagines embarrassment, then starts with ordinary friendly talk and finds awkwardness is normal.

passage: Come here, beta, and sit. You asked how I knew what to say to you last week, so I'll tell you. I'm Pooja. I was sixteen then, and there was a girl in my class called Vasudha. Whenever she walked into the room my whole body noticed. I didn't know what that pull meant. I only knew my family had a picture of my future, and I couldn't tell if this fit inside it. I didn't tell anyone for months, and I kept trying to name it and getting scared. Finally I told my cousin Reena, who only said, "You don't have to know today." I can still remember how my shoulders dropped. I took my time. I stayed honest with myself and I didn't rush to any label. That patience is what I'm giving you now.

qa.q: What was the name of the girl in Pooja's class?
qa.a: Her name was Vasudha.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling in those months, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Confused and worried. Pooja did not know what the pull meant, could not tell if it fit the family's picture of the future, and kept trying to name it and getting scared.

qa.q: What helped Pooja most, and what does it suggest a wise person might do?
qa.a: Telling cousin Reena, who said Pooja did not have to know today, helped. Talking to someone trusted and taking time worked better than rushing to a label.

qa.q: How might Reena have seen Pooja's confession?
qa.a: Reena probably wanted Pooja to feel safe rather than pushed, which is why Reena said Pooja didn't have to know that day.

grounding: Pooja felt a strong pull toward a classmate and was unsure what it meant or how it fit family expectations; Pooja took time and confided in someone trusted.

passage: In the school music room after practice, Naveen packed his guitar slowly, watching Suraj tune the tabla and glance at the door where Anaya had just left. It had been two weeks since Naveen realised his friend liked her too. Since then he'd felt something sour: he'd started to hurry to sit beside her, and yesterday he had caught himself hoping Suraj would say something silly in front of her. He hated that thought. "Suraj," he said, and his voice came out rough. "I like Anaya. I think you do too. I don't want that to mess us up." Suraj went still, then laughed with relief. "I thought you'd be angry. Honestly, you're my best friend, more than any crush." They shook on it, awkwardly, and finished packing together.

qa.q: Where do Naveen and Suraj have their conversation?
qa.a: They talk in the school music room after practice.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling before he spoke to Suraj?
qa.a: Sour rivalry and shame. He noticed he was hurrying to sit beside Anaya and had hoped Suraj would say something silly in front of her, and he hated that thought.

qa.q: Why was speaking honestly early a good choice for Naveen?
qa.a: It stopped the rivalry from turning into secret undermining and put the friendship ahead of the crush.

qa.q: How did Suraj see the moment?
qa.a: He felt relieved, since he had expected Naveen to be angry. He says Naveen matters more to him than any crush.

grounding: Naveen's friend likes the same person and rivalry creeps in, so Naveen speaks honestly early and values the friendship above the crush.

passage: Pranav had stopped counting how many times Vidya said, "If you loved me, you'd show me." First it was his phone password, then the group chat, then which shirt he should wear to Manu's birthday. "Not the blue one," she said. "Girls look at you in it." On Sunday when his friends called him for cricket, her messages piled up, angry, until he cancelled. That evening Manu texted, "You've gone quiet, yaar." Pranav stared at the screen. He realised he was afraid to put his phone down, and that being afraid didn't feel like love. He told Manu he was coming to cricket the next weekend. Then he showed his elder cousin Deepa the messages. "This is control," she said quietly. "It isn't your fault. Let's talk to your mother."

qa.q: What was the first thing Vidya asked Pranav for?
qa.a: She asked for his phone password.

qa.q: What did Pranav realise as he stared at the screen after Manu's text?
qa.a: He realised he was afraid to put his phone down and that being afraid did not feel like love.

qa.q: What steps did Pranav take that helped him?
qa.a: He stayed in touch with his friend Manu, planned to go to cricket, and showed his cousin Deepa the messages so a trusted adult could help.

qa.q: How might Manu have seen Pranav's silence?
qa.a: Manu noticed Pranav had gone quiet and seems worried about Pranav, so Manu reached out with a friendly text.

grounding: Pranav's partner demands his password, tells him what to wear and gets angry when he sees friends; he names it as control and tells a trusted person.

passage:
Day 1. Hafsa said she couldn't skip her cousin's engagement dinner on Saturday. Noor's reply came fast: "So I don't matter. You're selfish. I'll fall apart without you." Hafsa's chest tightened. She typed three apologies and deleted them. She felt she had done something terrible.

Day 5. She gave in and told her mother she was ill. The whole evening she watched Noor's messages and felt hollow, not relieved. Noor was warm again, and Hafsa noticed how the warmth came only after she gave in.

Day 12. When Noor started again about another plan, Hafsa wrote, "I care about you, and I'm still going." It hurt. She went to Ms Iyer, the school counsellor, and told her all of it. "You can be kind to Noor and still say no," Ms Iyer said. "Let's keep talking."

qa.q: Which event did Hafsa say she could not skip on Day 1?
qa.a: She could not skip her cousin's engagement dinner on Saturday.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel after giving in on Day 5?
qa.a: Hollow, not relieved. She noticed that Noor's warmth only came back after she gave in.

qa.q: What did Hafsa do differently on Day 12?
qa.a: She wrote that she cared but was still going, and she talked to the school counsellor Ms Iyer, which is care without giving in plus help from a trusted adult.

qa.q: How might Noor see the situation?
qa.a: Noor may truly feel scared of losing Hafsa, but pressure that blames her for Noor's feelings is not fair to either of them.

grounding: Noor calls Hafsa selfish and says they will fall apart when she resists; over days she moves from guilt and giving in to caring while holding her ground and seeking a counsellor.

passage: I want to say this out loud because it took me almost a year to see it. I'm Sangeeta. With Gopika, I learned to read her face at the classroom door before I even said hello. If her jaw was tight I'd say less, laugh less and check my phone for what I'd forgotten. Her anger came fast, like a slammed door, and afterwards she'd be sweet again. My stomach hurt every evening before her calls. I told myself I was just careless. Then my science teacher noticed I'd stopped eating lunch with my friends and asked if I was okay. I said no, for the first time. She helped me phone a helpline with my mother sitting next to me. It's not my fault, and I'm working on believing it. We're planning together how I can leave safely.

qa.q: Whose face did Sangeeta learn to read at the classroom door?
qa.a: Sangeeta learned to read Gopika's face.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling in the evenings before Gopika's calls?
qa.a: Dread. Sangeeta's stomach hurt, and Sangeeta blamed carelessness, which shows how much Sangeeta was tiptoeing around Gopika's mood.

qa.q: What helped Sangeeta take a first step?
qa.a: Sangeeta answered no when the science teacher asked, then phoned a helpline with Sangeeta's mother alongside and started planning a safe way out.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta's teacher have seen Sangeeta before that conversation?
qa.a: Worried. Sangeeta had stopped eating lunch with friends, so the teacher noticed the change and asked kindly.

grounding: Sangeeta tiptoes around a partner's mood and dreads explosions, recognises it is not Sangeeta's fault and turns to a teacher, Sangeeta's mother and a helpline.

passage: The engagement party in Nitin's village had one bar of network, and only on the roof. Varun sat at home with his phone clutched to his chest. Four messages, no reply. His heart pounded as if someone were chasing him. He typed a fifth: "Are you there? Why are you ignoring me?" His thumb stopped above send. It felt like he would die if he didn't hear back. But some corner of his mind asked whether that was really love or whether it was fear, and he put the phone face down on the bed. He went to his elder brother Chirag, who was fixing a bicycle, and said, "I can't stop. I keep needing to check." Chirag handed him a spanner. "Talk to me. And maybe the counsellor at school." Varun held the wheel and breathed.

qa.q: Why did Varun have so little contact with Nitin that evening?
qa.a: The engagement party in Nitin's village had only one bar of network, and only on the roof.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling as he held the phone, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Panic. His heart pounded as if someone were chasing him, and it felt like he would die if he did not hear back.

qa.q: What did Varun do that was wise?
qa.a: He did not send the fifth message. He put the phone face down, told his brother Chirag what was happening and accepted the idea of seeing the school counsellor.

qa.q: How might Nitin see the flood of messages?
qa.a: Nitin would probably feel crowded or pressured, especially while trying to enjoy a family party, so holding back protects them both.

grounding: Varun feels he will die without his partner and needs constant reassurance, recognises it as anxiety, does not monitor Nitin, and seeks support.
